A few rules-of-thumb for quick reference

 

In words that Dutch shares with its West-Germanic brethren, the F has changed into V and the S into Z (This seems to have codified into writing somewhere in the early 1600s. In older texts — I'm hardly an expert btw — this wasn't the case yet.)

  • English: friend, flesh, sea, salt

  • Dutch: vriend, vlees, zee, zout (NB "ou" where English and German have "al" is also not uncommon)

  • German: Freund, Fleisch, See, Salz (actually See means 'lake' rather than 'sea', but it is obviously the same word)

 

English words (of germanic root) with a th (especially a voiceless th but sometimes also a voiced one), often have a d in Dutch :

  • English: thousand, thorn, thumb

  • Dutch: duizend, doorn, duim

 

The g is almost always, and the ch is very often, a fricative sound (g is voiced, ch voiceless, usually; some dialects have no voiced sounds though, notably that of Amsterdam).

 

Dutch, like German, weaves words together much more often than English: keukendoor vs. 'kitchen door'

 

Numeral compound words are more systematic in English (but because native speakers of English usually use imperial units — arguable the single great flaw of the Anglosophere — this potential advantage is wasted anyway). In Dutch it is done like in English in the time of Shakespeare:

  • English: twenty five

  • Archaic English: five-and-twenty

  • Dutch: vijfentwintig

  • Mild dutch swearing involves the English loanwords shit and fuck . I kid you not.
